generatedProse.concept-context: In psychology, this connected view is how you make sense of any study you meet, from a lecture reading to a journal article. You look for the research question, see how the study was designed and limited, and follow the method, results and discussion through to what was found. Held together, the three strands turn a dense psychology paper into something you can actually follow.
generatedProse.worked-example: Tom and Amara both read the same memory experiment for a seminar. Tom skips to the results, reads the numbers, and leaves unsure what the study was even asking. Amara finds the research question first, sees how the sample and task were chosen and limited, and follows the method, results and discussion through to the findings. Reading the paper as one connected whole, Amara can explain what it showed; Tom cannot.
generatedProse.summary: Research in psychology makes most sense when you see it as one connected whole. A research question becomes a designed study, and that study takes a recognisable shape on the page, carrying it from question to findings. It is this connected view, not any single part on its own, that helps you read psychology research across your degree.

check.body: A student reads a journal article. They spot the focused question in the introduction, notice how the study was shaped and limited, and follow the method, results and discussion through to the findings. What does this show?

items.text: Their next round of learning and preparation, which is why the following report improved.
Nothing; feedback comes at the end, so it cannot affect anything that follows.
Only the mark on the first report, which cannot now change.
The deadline for the next report.

feedback.correct: That's right. Using the feedback fed back into the next round of learning and preparation, which is why the following report improved: that is the cycle working.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. Think about what the student changed before the next report, not the old mark or the deadline.
feedback.incorrectFinal: Using the feedback fed back into the student's next round of learning and preparation, which is why the next report improved. The old mark cannot change and the deadline is not part of the cycle; feedback is not the end, it feeds the next turn.

_items.text: That they are reading research as one connected whole, using the three strands together to follow it from question to findings.
_items.feedback: Yes. The three strands worked together as one view of the whole project.

_items.text: That the article was too simple to count as real research.
_items.feedback: Spotting the parts does not make the research simple; it shows the strands working together.

_items.text: That only the introduction matters when you read research.
_items.feedback: Each part did a job here, not just the introduction.

_items.text: That the student was only interested in the final results.
_items.feedback: They followed the whole thread, from the question through to the findings.
